text:
The passage rewards the reader who attends to what is missing from it. Sarah is nowhere in the chapter, and the book announces her death in the verse immediately following; the scene implies, without saying so, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, in Genesis 22; Isaac is not mentioned. At precisely the point where a lesser story would linger, the narrative turns away. The silence is more than absence; it has the force of testimony.

An opposed account may say that the chapter simply observes the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports characters' feelings and never explains. This, perhaps, in some sense, may be true. Yet the narrator elsewhere gives feeling plainly enough: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate. The text knows what it is doing. Restraint, in this voice, is a kind of accusation.
